claim: VGluT3 expression within hippocampal interneuron terminals is minimal during early development (postnatal day 5, P5), but progressively increases during juvenile to adult stages.
source: In contrast, native VGluT3 expression within hippocampal interneuron terminals is minimal during early development (postnatal day 5, P5), but progressively increases during juvenile to adult stages (Figure 1A, see also Gras et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by immunolocalization data shown in Figure 1A and cited reference (Gras et al., 2005)

claim: VGluT3 immunosignal is present within presynaptic boutons delineated by strong cannabinoid receptor 1 (CBR1) labeling in CA1 stratum pyramidale.
source: Indeed, high-resolution imaging within CA1 stratum pyramidale (s.p.) confirmed VGluT3 immunosignal within presynaptic boutons delineated by strong cannabinoid receptor 1 (CBR1) labeling, a signature of CCK+BC terminals (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by high-resolution imaging data shown in Figure 1B

claim: VGluT3 signal exhibits essentially complete overlap with VGAT and GAD67 in stratum pyramidale.
source: In addition, s.p. VGluT3 signal exhibited essentially complete overlap with VGAT and GAD67 (Figure 1B), confirming that the signal derives from local circuit interneurons.
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1B

claim: VGluT3 did not colocalize with synaptotagmin 2 (Syt2) containing terminals in stratum pyramidale.
source: As a negative control, we confirmed that VGluT3 did not colocalize with synaptotagmin 2 (Syt2) containing terminals in s.p. which delineate perisomatic inputs from parvalbumin expressing BCs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1B

claim: VGluT3 expression is conserved at all putative release sites along continuous individual axon segments.
source: Moreover, evaluation of multiple boutons along individual parent axons suggests uniform distribution of VGluT3 at all terminals of VGluT3+ interneurons minimizing the potential for postsynaptic target cell specificity to any glutamatergic phenotype of CCK+VGluT3+INTS (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by axon segment analysis shown in Figure 1C-D

claim: Developmental characterization of hippocampal CA1/CA3 cells reported by red fluorescent protein expression (RFP+) in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 transgenic mice recapitulated the delayed onset of native VGluT3 expression with low cell densities reported early postnatally that increase and plateau through juvenile stages into adulthood.
source: Developmental characterization of hippocampal CA1/CA3 cells reported by red fluorescent protein expression (RFP+) in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 transgenic mice recapitulated the delayed onset of native VGluT3 expression with low cell densities reported early postnatally that increase and plateau through juvenile stages into adulthood (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by developmental profiling data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Cajal Retzius cells within the dentate molecular layer along the hippocampal fissure are reported in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice throughout postnatal development, but particularly at the earliest stages.
source: Throughout postnatal development, but particularly at the earliest stages, Cajal Retzius cells within the dentate molecular layer along the hippocampal fissure are also reported (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Within the neocortex a subpopulation of deep layer RFP+ pyramidal cells is observed in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice, consistent with recently described 'Slc17a8+ L5 pyramidal cells'.
source: In addition, within the neocortex a subpopulation of deep layer RFP+ pyramidal cells is observed, consistent with recently described 'Slc17a8+ L5 pyramidal cells' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and cited reference (Tasic et al., 2018)

claim: Within CA1, excellent registration was observed between the distributions of VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported and CCK immunoreactive cells.
source: Indeed, within CA1 we observed excellent registration between the distributions of VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported and CCK immunoreactive cells and confirmed that the vast majority of genetically identified cells are CCK+ (~80%; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The vast majority of VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported cells in CA1 are CCK+ (~80%).
source: Indeed, within CA1 we observed excellent registration between the distributions of VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported and CCK immunoreactive cells and confirmed that the vast majority of genetically identified cells are CCK+ (~80%; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B

claim: VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported cells comprised almost half of all CCK+ CA1 interneurons.
source: Conversely, VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported cells comprised almost half of all CCK+ CA1 interneurons, considerably higher than original estimates in rat (~25%) but similar to estimates in mouse (~46%) based on immunohistochemical (IHC) studies (Del Pino et al., 2017; Somogyi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by quantification data and comparison to cited references (Del Pino et al., 2017; Somogyi et al., 2004)

claim: RFP+ cells in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice rarely exhibited PV immunoreactivity.
source: Similarly, RFP+ cells rarely exhibited PV immunoreactivity (Figure 2B), consistent with the lack of VGluT3/Syt2 colocalization in perisomatic targeting terminals (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1B

claim: Somatostatin (Som) expression was observed within a minority (~20%) of RFP+ cells in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice, particularly within stratum oriens.
source: Unexpectedly, we regularly observed somatostatin (Som) expression within a minority (~20%) of RFP+ cells, particularly within s.o. (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Native VGluT3 mRNA expression was validated within a small subset of Som interneurons of the mature hippocampus.
source: However, we validated native VGluT3 mRNA expression within a small subset of Som interneurons of the mature hippocampus and confirmed active Cre in Som+ cells reported in adult VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; see also Sst.Erbb4.RGS10 and Sst.Pnoc.Pvalb single-cell RNASeq-based clusters in Harris et al. (2018).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and Cre expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and cited reference (Harris et al., 2018)

claim: The temporal profile of interneuron reporting in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice faithfully recapitulates normal delayed VGluT3 production.
source: Importantly, the temporal profile of interneuron reporting faithfully recapitulates normal delayed VGluT3 production and indicates that functional interrogation of physiological roles for VGluT3 within these cells is best performed in mature animals beyond 1 month of age.
evidence: Based on inference from developmental profiling data

claim: A high proportion of VGluT3 lacking RFP+ perisomatic terminals in young VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice is consistent with delayed VGluT3 accumulation in preexisting axons.
source: Indeed, a high proportion of VGluT3 lacking RFP+ perisomatic terminals in young VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice is consistent with delayed VGluT3 accumulation in preexisting axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by terminal colocalization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: The proportion of VGluT3+ CB1R+ perisomatic terminals significantly increases from postnatal days 10 to 90 with no significant increase in overall CB1R+ terminal density.
source: Moreover, the proportion of VGluT3+ CB1R+ perisomatic terminals significantly increases from postnatal days 10 to 90 with no significant increase in overall CB1R+ terminal density consistent with delayed accumulation of VGluT3 in a subset of hippocampal resident CCK+BCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Evaluation of individual RFP+ interneurons from VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice revealed a much broader diversity of cell morphologies including basket cells and diverse dendrite targeting interneurons.
source: However, evaluation of individual RFP+ interneurons from VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice revealed a much broader diversity of cell morphologies. Post-hoc recovered anatomies following electrophysiological recordings from CA1/3 RFP+ cells in acute slices revealed BCs as well as diverse dendrite targeting interneurons (DTIs) such as Schaffer collateral associated cells, perforant path associated cells, and mossy fiber associated cells (Figure 3A; see also Lasztóczi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data shown in Figure 3A and cited reference (Lasztóczi et al., 2011)

claim: VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported BCs displayed mature axon profiles as early as P13.
source: Interestingly, VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 reported BCs displayed mature axon profiles as early as P13 supporting the conclusion of delayed VGluT3 expression within anatomically mature BCs rather than delayed axon extension following VGluT3 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: A subset of VGluT3+ terminals within CA1 stratum radiatum colocalized with CB1R and VGAT.
source: Consistent with VGluT3 expressing DTIs we observed that a subset of VGluT3+ terminals within CA1 s.r. colocalized with CB1R, and VGAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: A population of large VGluT3+ terminals, particularly enriched along the stratum radiatum-stratum lacunosum moleculare border, were CB1R-/VGAT- but often expressed vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2+) consistent with raphe serotonergic fibers.
source: In contrast, a population of large VGluT3+ terminals, particularly enriched along the s.r.-stratum lacunosum moleculare (s.l.m.) border, were CB1R-/VGAT- but often expressed vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2+) consistent with raphe serotonergic fibers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The VGluT3+ subset of CA1/3 CCK+ interneurons extends beyond BCs encompassing the entire known spectrum of CCK+ interneurons.
source: Thus, the VGluT3+ subset of CA1/3 CCK+ interneurons extends beyond BCs encompassing the entire known spectrum of CCK+ interneurons (reviewed in Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on anatomical diversity observed and cited review (Pelkey et al., 2017)

claim: CCK+VGluT3+ BCs and DTIs exhibit remarkably homogeneous active and passive membrane properties.
source: Despite their considerable anatomical heterogeneity, CCK+VGluT3+INTS exhibited remarkably homogeneous active and passive membrane properties. Both BCs and DTIs consistently displayed high input resistances, slow time constants, hyperpolarization-induced sag, and regular accommodating firing patterns typical of CCK+ interneurons (e.g. traces in Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A and Table 1

claim: No significant differences were detected between VGluT3+ BCs and DTIs across a broad range of biophysical features.
source: Indeed, we failed to detect any significant differences between VGluT3+ BCs and DTIs across a broad range of biophysical features (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Table 1

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC pairs yielded uIPSCs with high inter-event amplitude variability, modest short-term depression, and train-induced asynchronous release.
source: CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC pairs yielded uIPSCs with high inter-event amplitude variability, modest short-term depression, and train-induced asynchronous release (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by paired recording data shown in Figure 3B-C

claim: Transmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS was susceptible to depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI).
source: Moreover, transmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS was susceptible to depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition (DSI), consistent with the expression of CB1Rs within presynaptic terminals of VGluT3+ BCs and DTIs (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Supported by DSI data shown in Figure 3D-E

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INTS reported in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice exhibit all the hallmark features expected for CCK+ interneuron-mediated inhibition.
source: Thus, CCK+VGluT3+INTS reported in VGluT3-Cre:Ai14 mice exhibit all the hallmark features expected for CCK+ interneuron-mediated inhibition (Armstrong and Soltesz, 2012; Daw et al., 2009; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Wyeth et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison to cited references (Armstrong and Soltesz, 2012; Daw et al., 2009; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Wyeth et al., 2017)

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC pairs yielded amplitudes/potencies within the low range of those reported in prior studies of CCK+ interneurons that did not selectively target the VGluT3+ subsets.
source: Interestingly, CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC pairs yielded amplitudes/potencies within the low range of those reported in prior studies of CCK+ interneurons that did not selectively target the VGluT3+ subsets (Daw et al., 2009; Kohus et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Vargish et al., 2017; Wyeth et al., 2017); note that in some cases differences in Cl- driving force must be accounted for).
evidence: Based on comparison to cited references (Daw et al., 2009; Kohus et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2010; Vargish et al., 2017; Wyeth et al., 2017)

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INTS do not appear to exhibit enhanced GABA release compared to the general population of CCK+ BCs and DTIs.
source: Thus, CCK+VGluT3+INTS do not appear to exhibit enhanced GABA release compared to the general population of CCK+ BCs and DTIs, arguing against a role for VGluT3 in facilitating SV GABA filling through 'vesicular synergy' (Amilhon et al., 2010; El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Fasano et al., 2017; Frahm et al., 2015; Gras et al., 2008; Hnasko et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on comparison to prior studies and cited references (Amilhon et al., 2010; El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Fasano et al., 2017; Frahm et al., 2015; Gras et al., 2008; Hnasko et al., 2010)

claim: A recent study in the amygdala failed to observe enhanced unitary transmission from VGluT3+ CCK interneurons over those lacking VGluT3.
source: Similarly, a recent study in the amygdala failed to observe enhanced unitary transmission from VGluT3+ CCK interneurons over those lacking VGluT3 (Rovira-Esteban et al., 2017) and forced VGluT3 expression in cultured striatal GABAergic interneurons failed to facilitate quantal GABA transmission (Zimmermann et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Rovira-Esteban et al., 2017; Zimmermann et al., 2015)

claim: DSI sensitivity of release from CCK+VGluT3+INTS is comparable to that of the general CCK+ interneuron population.
source: However, DSI sensitivity of release from CCK+VGluT3+INTS is comparable to that of the general CCK+ interneuron population (Daw et al., 2009; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Vargish et al., 2017; Wyeth et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison to cited references (Daw et al., 2009; Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Vargish et al., 2017; Wyeth et al., 2017)

claim: Functional α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) are abundantly expressed within PC somatic membranes.
source: Although the perisomatic domain of hippocampal PCs is devoid of conventional excitatory synapses (Megías et al., 2001), functional α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) are abundantly expressed within PC somatic membranes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; and see for eg. Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Jonas and Sakmann, 1992; Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited references (Megías et al., 2001; Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Jonas and Sakmann, 1992; Lu et al., 2009)

claim: Both VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos optogenetic strategies yielded large light-evoked outward synaptic currents under control conditions confirming GABA as the dominant transmitter.
source: Both optogenetic strategies yielded large light-evoked outward synaptic currents under control conditions at the beginning of all recordings confirming GABA as the dominant transmitter (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data shown in Figure 4B-C

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GABARs with a combination of picrotoxin, bicuculline, and CGP 55845 consistently uncovered a residual small inward synaptic conductance.
source: However, pharmacological inhibition of GABARs with a combination of picrotoxin, bicuculline, and CGP 55845 (pic/bic/CGP) consistently uncovered a residual small inward synaptic conductance (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data shown in Figure 4B-C

claim: The pic/bic/CGP-insensitive light-evoked events exhibited linear current-voltage relations with reversal near 0 mV and rapid decay kinetics compared to the corresponding GABAergic events.
source: Consistent with mediation by AMPARs, the residual light-evoked inward synaptic currents exhibited linear current-voltage relations with reversal near 0 mV and rapid decay kinetics compared to the corresponding GABAergic events (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by current-voltage relation and kinetic data shown in Figure 4D-E

claim: The pic/bic/CGP-insensitive light-evoked events displayed pharmacological profiles typical of AMPARs including prolonged decays following block of receptor desensitization with cyclothiazide (CTZ) and antagonism by DNQX, GYKI, or γ-DGG.
source: Moreover, the pic/bic/CGP-insensitive light-evoked events displayed pharmacological profiles typical of AMPARs including prolonged decays following block of receptor desensitization with cyclothiazide (CTZ) and antagonism by DNQX, GYKI, or γ-DGG (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 4E-F

claim: No glutamatergic component to transmission was associated with light-evoked transmission in Nkx2.1-Cre:Ai32 mice.
source: Importantly, no glutamatergic component to transmission was associated with light-evoked transmission in Nkx2.1-Cre:Ai32 mice that express ChR2 in medial ganglionic eminence derived interneurons which excludes CCK+ cells, confirming that light activation of hippocampal interneurons does not generally promote glutamate release nonspecifically (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by control optogenetic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The perfect register between GABA and glutamate PSC latencies is consistent with a common presynaptic source for both transmitters.
source: However, the perfect register between GABA and glutamate PSC latencies is consistent with a common presynaptic source for both transmitters (Figure 4B inset).
evidence: Supported by latency data shown in Figure 4B inset

claim: The complete overlap between VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos data sets argues in favor of local hippocampal CCK+VGluT3+INTS in mediating both responses.
source: Moreover, the complete overlap between VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos data sets argues in favor of local hippocampal CCK+VGluT3+INTS in mediating both responses (Figure 4B–I).
evidence: Based on comparison of data from two optogenetic strategies shown in Figure 4B-I

claim: The GABAergic and glutamatergic light-evoked synaptic events in VGluT3Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3Cre:Chronos mice exhibit prominent DSI.
source: Indeed, the GABAergic and glutamatergic light-evoked synaptic events in VGluT3Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3Cre:Chronos mice exhibit prominent DSI as expected for synaptic events derived from CCK+VGluT3+INTS endowed with presynaptic CB1Rs (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: Supported by DSI data shown in Figure 4G-I

claim: An AMPAR-mediated component was observed in 17/53 synaptically coupled CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC paired recordings.
source: Using this strategy, we observed an AMPAR-mediated component in 17/53 synaptically coupled CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC paired recordings (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: Supported by paired recording data shown in Figure 4J-L

claim: In the majority of pairs exhibiting AMPAR-mediated transmission, the GABA to glutamate transition was directly monitored (12/17) unequivocally illustrating GABA and glutamate corelease from individual CCK+VGluT3+INTS onto the same postsynaptic partner.
source: In the majority of pairs exhibiting AMPAR-mediated transmission, we directly monitored the GABA to glutamate transition (12/17, connected points in Figure 4K; remainder obtained following pic/bic/CGP) unequivocally illustrating GABA and glutamate corelease from individual CCK+VGluT3+INTS onto the same postsynaptic partner.
evidence: Supported by paired recording data shown in Figure 4K

claim: Following 2–4 hr of SCZ incubation GABAergic output from CCK+VGluT3+INTS was severely compromised often allowing glutamatergic output to be observed even prior to pic/bic/CGP treatment.
source: Following 2–4 hr of SCZ incubation GABAergic output from CCK+VGluT3+INTS was severely compromised often allowing glutamatergic output to be observed even prior to pic/bic/CGP treatment (e.g. traces in Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data with SCZ treatment shown in Figure 5A

claim: SCZ treatment resulted in impaired GABAergic signaling coupled with almost a doubling of the AMPAR-mediated synaptic conductance, yielding a dramatic reduction in the GABA/glutamate ratio of CCK+VGluT3+INT transmission.
source: Overall, the impaired GABAergic signaling coupled with almost a doubling of the AMPAR-mediated synaptic conductance (evaluated in pic/bic/CGP plus the cocktail), yielded a dramatic reduction in the GABA/glutamate ratio of CCK+VGluT3+INT transmission (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data with SCZ treatment shown in Figure 5A

claim: In SCZ-treated slices without AM 251 on board the glutamatergic phenotype of light-evoked events retained DSI sensitivity.
source: Importantly, in SCZ-treated slices without AM 251 on board the glutamatergic phenotype of light-evoked events retained DSI sensitivity consistent with SCZ treatment promoting glutamate release from CB1R expressing CCK+VGluT3+INTS rather than uncovering a novel source (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by DSI data in SCZ-treated slices shown in Figure 5B

claim: Enhanced glutamatergic events in SCZ-treated slices could be inhibited by the CB1R agonist WIN-55212–2 at a high dose (5 µM) to overcome the antagonistic effects of AM 251 (2 µM).
source: Indeed, enhanced glutamatergic events in SCZ-treated slices could be inhibited by the CB1R agonist WIN-55212–2 at a high dose (5 µM) to overcome the antagonistic effects of AM 251 (2 µM) normally present in our cocktail (26.6 ± 0.1% of control, n = 5, p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological data with WIN-55212-2

claim: Enhanced glutamatergic transmission was evident in a limited data set evaluated with CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC paired recordings in SCZ treated slices.
source: Moreover, enhanced glutamatergic transmission was evident in a limited data set evaluated with CCK+VGluT3+INT-CA1PC paired recordings in SCZ treated slices (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by paired recording data in SCZ-treated slices shown in Figure 5C

claim: Optogenetic evaluation of mice kept on the B6- diet for 3–9 months revealed reduced GABAergic transmission with increased glutamatergic transmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS compared to littermates maintained on a control diet (B6+).
source: Optogenetic evaluation of mice kept on the B6- diet for 3–9 months revealed reduced GABAergic transmission with increased glutamatergic transmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS compared to littermates maintained on a control diet (B6+) leading to a significantly depressed GABA/glutamate synaptic conductance ratio (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data from B6- diet mice shown in Figure 5D

claim: Under basal conditions, optogenetic activation of slices from VGluT3Cre:Ai32 mice was highly effective in suppressing network activity.
source: With inhibition intact (i.e. no GABA or GAD antagonists) optogenetic activation of slices from VGluT3Cre:Ai32 mice was highly effective in suppressing network activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by local field potential recording data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In approximately 20% of the optogenetic recordings performed in the drug cocktail polysynaptic network barrages were observed following short duration single-pulse light-evoked monosynaptic signaling.
source: In contrast, in approximately 20% of the optogenetic recordings performed in our drug cocktail polysynaptic network barrages were observed following short duration single-pulse light-evoked monosynaptic signaling (e.g. Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Polysynaptic network events observed in both VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos mice were blocked by CB1R activation with WIN-55212–2.
source: Importantly, polysynaptic network events observed in both VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos mice were blocked by CB1R activation with WIN-55212–2 consistent with the events being triggered by CCK+VGluT3+INTS (Figure 5E,G).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5E,G

claim: All the basic features of optogenetically driven glutamatergic signaling observed in VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos mice, including triggering of polysynaptic network activity, were observed in slices from VGluT3-Cre mice injected with a viral vector encoding Cre-dependent and interneuron-specific ChR2.
source: Moreover, all the basic features of optogenetically driven glutamatergic signaling observed in VGluT3-Cre:Ai32 and VGluT3-Cre:Chronos mice, including triggering of polysynaptic network activity, were observed in slices from VGluT3-Cre mice injected with a viral vector encoding Cre-dependent and interneuron-specific ChR2 (Figure 5H–L; VGluT3-Cre:AAV-mDlx-Flex-ChR2; Dimidschstein et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic recording data with viral ChR2 expression shown in Figure 5H-L and cited reference (Dimidschstein et al., 2016)

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INTS have the capacity to trigger paradoxical network excitation.
source: Thus, CCK+VGluT3+INTS have the capacity to trigger paradoxical network excitation.
evidence: Based on inference from polysynaptic network activity data

claim: No prior study has provided direct evidence for VGluT3-mediated vesicular synergy of GABA filling or glutamate cotransmission within CCK+VGluT3+INTS.
source: However, no prior study has provided direct evidence for VGluT3-mediated vesicular synergy of GABA filling or glutamate cotransmission within CCK+VGluT3+INTS.
evidence: Based on review of prior literature

claim: A recent study observed reduced miniature IPSC (mIPSC) amplitudes following genetic ablation of VGluT3 generally or selectively within interneurons.
source: A recent study observed reduced miniature IPSC (mIPSC) amplitudes following genetic ablation of VGluT3 generally or selectively within interneurons and interpreted the findings to reflect reduced SV GABA filling within CCK+VGluT3+INTS (Fasano et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Fasano et al., 2017)

claim: Loss of VGluT3 (both generally and specifically in interneurons) increased mIPSC frequency and enhanced IPSCs evoked with bulk electrical stimulation.
source: In the same study, loss of VGluT3 (both generally and specifically in interneurons) increased mIPSC frequency and enhanced IPSCs evoked with bulk electrical stimulation (Fasano et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Fasano et al., 2017)

claim: mGluR4 antagonism enhanced evoked IPSCs (and mIPSC frequency) in wild type but not VGluT3 knockout mice.
source: Indeed, mGluR4 antagonism enhanced evoked IPSCs (and mIPSC frequency) in wild type but not VGluT3 knockout mice indirectly implicating glutamate release from CCK+VGluT3+INTS in regulating GABA release.
evidence: Based on inference from cited findings

claim: The study directly confirms GABA and glutamate cotransmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS through complementary optogenetic and synaptically coupled paired recording approaches.
source: Here, we directly confirm GABA and glutamate cotransmission from CCK+VGluT3+INTS through complementary optogenetic and synaptically coupled paired recording approaches.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic and paired recording data throughout the manuscript

claim: VGluT3 expression in CCK+VGluT3+INTS exhibits a delayed developmental onset in contrast with neuronal populations that transiently express VGluT3 early in development during synaptogenesis or refinement.
source: Importantly, we found that VGluT3 expression in CCK+VGluT3+INTS exhibits a delayed developmental onset in contrast with neuronal populations that transiently express VGluT3 early in development during synaptogenesis or refinement (Noh et al., 2010; Peirs et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by developmental profiling data and cited references (Noh et al., 2010; Peirs et al., 2015)

claim: Under basal conditions, the glutamatergic component of CCK+VGluT3+INT-mediated transmission is absolutely dwarfed by the GABAergic component.
source: Moreover, under basal conditions, the glutamatergic component of CCK+VGluT3+INT-mediated transmission is absolutely dwarfed by the GABAergic component.
evidence: Supported by paired recording and optogenetic data showing dominant GABAergic transmission

claim: CCK+VGluT3+INTS account for only 7% of hippocampal interneurons (roughly half of all CCK+ interneurons).
source: We estimate that CCK+VGluT3+INTS account for only 7% of hippocampal interneurons (roughly half of all CCK+ interneurons, current findings and see Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013), yet this cohort exhibits profound influence over network excitability.
evidence: Based on quantification data and cited reference (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013)

claim: Under basal conditions, the powerful GABAergic inhibition provided by CCK+VGluT3+INTS can be harnessed to dramatically dampen circuit excitability as evidenced by complete suppression of gamma oscillations.
source: Under basal conditions, the powerful GABAergic inhibition provided by CCK+VGluT3+INTS can be harnessed to dramatically dampen circuit excitability as evidenced by complete suppression of gamma oscillations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by local field potential recording data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Following amplification of their glutamatergic phenotype CCK+VGluT3+INTS can promote paradoxical network hyperexcitability which may be relevant to disorders associated with GAD dysfunction such as schizophrenia, depression, and Huntington's Disease as well as nutritional deficiencies in the co-enzyme pyridoxine (vitamin B6).
source: However, following amplification of their glutamatergic phenotype CCK+VGluT3+INTS can promote paradoxical network hyperexcitability which may be relevant to disorders associated with GAD dysfunction such as schizophrenia, depression, and Huntington's Disease as well as nutritional deficiencies in the co-enzyme pyridoxine (vitamin B6) (de Jonge et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2018; Rush et al., 2012; Torrey et al., 2005).
